name: Germany
governanceModel: EU AI Act implemented nationally through the KI-MIG enforcement law
debateTopics: Executive liability risk under Germany's AI Act enforcement framework

Germany's sovereign AI champion merges with a foreign partner
overview:
Germany advanced AI Act implementing legislation in mid-2026: the KI-MIG — short for KI-Marktüberwachungs- und Innovationsförderungsgesetz (AI Market Surveillance and Innovation Promotion Act), Article 1 of the broader Act Implementing the AI Regulation (Gesetz zur Durchführung der KI-Verordnung) — passed the Bundestag on 11 June and was approved by the Bundesrat on 10 July, and reportedly entered into force on 29 July 2026 — days before the EU AI Act's 2 August 2026 milestone — naming the Bundesnetzagentur as Germany's central AI market-surveillance authority, national coordinator and single contact/complaints point (running an AI service desk and regulatory sandboxes), with BaFin covering financial-sector AI and BfDI retaining data-protection oversight. Some legal commentary has argued that existing German corporate-law doctrine could expose executives personally if they fail to implement adequate AI Act compliance oversight, though this appears to be a risk interpretation of general corporate law rather than an explicit personal-liability clause written into KI-MIG itself. Enforcement otherwise relies on the EU AI Act's own fine tiers — up to €35M or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices, and up to €15M or 3% for other high-risk violations — plus supplementary national fines of up to €50,000 under KI-MIG for cooperation and information-obligation breaches (this national-fine figure comes from secondary legal-commentary sources and has not been independently checked against the bill's primary text). Separately, at the EU level, the 'Digital Omnibus on AI' was adopted by the European Parliament and Council in June 2026, postponing most high-risk AI Act obligations from August 2026 to December 2027 (and product-embedded high-risk obligations to August 2028) — a delay that affects when KI-MIG's new enforcement powers will have substantive high-risk obligations to enforce. Dr. Karsten Wildberger has led the restructured Federal Ministry for Digital Transformation and Government Modernisation (BMDS), Germany's first dedicated digital ministry, since May 2025 and remained in the role as of mid-2026; Germany's National Security Council separately announced on 9 June 2026 that it intends to establish an AI safety institute modeled on the UK's AISI, though as of the most recent research no formal institute name, budget or legal basis had been confirmed.

Another notable German AI story in 2026 was industrial rather than regulatory: Aleph Alpha, sometimes described as Germany's sovereign answer to OpenAI and Mistral, agreed in April 2026 to merge with Canada's Cohere to form a combined transatlantic entity valued at roughly $20B, backed partly by a $600M investment from Germany's Schwarz Group. The deal had not closed as of the most recent research and remained subject to shareholder and regulatory approval — a development that sits alongside a new Germany-Canada Sovereign Technology Alliance launched in February 2026. Separately, SAP moved to acquire German startup Prior Labs in May 2026 (reported as completed around mid-July 2026) to build a frontier tabular-AI lab in Europe, distinct from the earlier, unrelated 'OpenAI for Germany' sovereign public-sector initiative SAP launched with OpenAI and Microsoft back in September 2025.

atAGlance.regulatoryApproach: KI-MIG implements and enforces the EU AI Act nationally; reportedly entered into force on 29 July 2026, making the Bundesnetzagentur the central national AI supervisory authority
atAGlance.latestMajorUpdate: A Munich court rules AI music generator Suno infringed GEMA-held copyright (training and output) on 31 July 2026, days after KI-MIG's reported 29 July entry into force and as the EU AI Act's GPAI-enforcement and transparency duties take effect on 2 August 2026
atAGlance.governmentInvolvement: Rising — new enforcement law advancing and a dedicated Digital Ministry in place since 2025
atAGlance.industrialStrategy: Balancing enforcement with competitiveness amid a national AI champion's merger with a foreign partner
atAGlance.internationalPartnerships: Germany-Canada Sovereign Technology Alliance (launched February 2026); full EU AI Act participation

currentDirection.summary: Germany moved from having no national AI-specific statute to standing up enforcement machinery within months: the KI-MIG — reportedly in force from 29 July 2026 — names the Bundesnetzagentur as central AI market-surveillance authority and adds modest national fines, and some legal commentators argue it heightens executives' exposure under existing German corporate-law doctrine even though the bill's own text does not appear to create a new personal-liability clause. This represents a tightening in enforcement posture even though the underlying substantive rules remain the EU AI Act's rather than a new German AI statute. At the same time, the EU's 2026 'Digital Omnibus on AI' postponed most high-risk AI Act obligations to late 2027/2028, so the near-term practical effect of this tightening on regulated businesses remains limited for now.

recentDevelopments.text: The EU AI Act's GPAI (general-purpose AI) supervision and enforcement powers, plus its Article 50 transparency duties (chatbot disclosure, AI-content marking and deepfake labelling), take effect on 2 August 2026; in Germany the newly designated Bundesnetzagentur acts as the national competent authority and complaints point, with BaFin overseeing AI-content marking and disclosure in the financial sector. Pre-existing systems reportedly have until 2 December 2026 for machine-readable watermarking, and most high-risk (Annex III) obligations were delayed to 2027–2028 under the EU's Digital Omnibus.

The Regional Court of Munich I reportedly rules that AI music generator Suno infringed copyright in works represented by German collecting society GEMA, in what is described as Europe's first such ruling: the court found six well-known works (including Alphaville's 'Forever Young' and Lou Bega's 'Mambo No. 5') reproducibly 'memorised' in Suno's v3.5 and v4 models and recognisable in their outputs, rejected a text-and-data-mining exception for training, and held Suno — not its users — liable for the infringing outputs, ordering disclosure of revenues and damages to be set later. The first-instance judgment is provisionally enforceable but not yet final; Suno may appeal to the Munich Higher Regional Court.

The KI-MIG (KI-Marktüberwachungs- und Innovationsförderungsgesetz — AI Market Surveillance and Innovation Promotion Act, Article 1 of the broader Act Implementing the AI Regulation) reportedly enters into force on 29 July 2026, following Bundestag passage on 11 June and Bundesrat approval on 10 July. It designates the Bundesnetzagentur as Germany's central AI market-surveillance authority, national coordinator and single contact/complaints point — running an AI service desk and regulatory sandboxes, and supervising sensitive areas such as employment and education directly — alongside BaFin (financial-sector AI) and BfDI (data protection). Enforcement draws on the EU AI Act's own fines (up to €35M or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices; up to €15M or 3% for other violations) plus KI-MIG's supplementary national fines of up to €50,000 for cooperation-obligation breaches.

Munich-based defense-AI company Helsing raises a $1.8B Series E at an $18B valuation, reportedly making it one of the most highly valued startups in mainland Europe; the company builds the HX-2 strike drone and Altra battlefield-AI software.

Germany's National Security Council decided on 9 June 2026 to establish a national AI safety institute — reported as being set up under the working title 'DE-AISI' — modeled on the UK's AI Safety Institute, to analyse frontier-model capabilities and risks (including testing models from labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI) and coordinate with peer institutes. It is reportedly designed initially as a 'virtual' institute drawing on the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) and the Bundesnetzagentur rather than a wholly new authority; formal budget and legal basis were still being worked out as of the most recent research, so 'DE-AISI' should be treated as a provisional label.

Cohere and Aleph Alpha announce a merger to create a combined transatlantic AI company valued at roughly $20B, backed partly by a $600M investment from Germany's Schwarz Group; the deal was not yet closed and remained subject to shareholder and regulatory approval.

Germany and Canada launch a Sovereign Technology Alliance on the margins of the Munich Security Conference via a Joint Declaration of Intent on AI signed by Digital Minister Karsten Wildberger and Canada's AI/Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon, building on a December 2025 Canada-Germany Digital Alliance.

SAP, OpenAI and Microsoft launch 'OpenAI for Germany,' a sovereign public-sector AI offering running on SAP's Delos Cloud subsidiary atop Azure infrastructure; first announced 24 September 2025, with pilot rollouts (including with the Max Planck Society) planned to begin in Q1 2026.

SAP announces the acquisition of German AI startup Prior Labs, committing to invest more than €1B over four years to build it into a frontier tabular-AI lab for Europe; Prior Labs continues to operate under its own brand and leadership within SAP, with the deal reported as completed around mid-July 2026.

Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) signs a roughly €19M framework agreement with Aleph Alpha for an internal AI helpdesk built on Pharia OS, intended to handle up to 90% of routine IT/HR inquiries.

Crunchbase News' coverage of European AI investment reportedly put German AI startup funding at roughly €1.7B in Q1 2026; the closest independently located figure is Crunchbase's separate report that Germany-based startups overall (not confirmed as AI-specific) raised about $1.9B in Q1 2026, which is roughly consistent in magnitude but does not clearly confirm that the €1.7B figure is AI-specific. Comparative claims about Germany's exact global ranking by AI startup count also could not be independently confirmed.

policyAndRegulation.title: KI-MIG (AI Market Surveillance and Innovation Promotion Act)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Passed by the Bundestag on 11 June 2026, approved by the Bundesrat on 10 July 2026, and reportedly in force from 29 July 2026 — days before the EU AI Act's 2 August 2026 milestone. KI-MIG (KI-Marktüberwachungs- und Innovationsförderungsgesetz) is Article 1 of the broader Act Implementing the AI Regulation (Gesetz zur Durchführung der KI-Verordnung); the file's earlier shorthand 'AI Act Implementing Act' described the umbrella law but was not KI-MIG's own name. The law designates the Bundesnetzagentur as Germany's central AI market-surveillance authority, national coordinator and single contact/complaints point (running an AI service desk and regulatory sandboxes, and supervising sensitive areas such as employment and education directly), with BaFin for financial-sector AI and BfDI for data protection, and adds supplementary national fines of up to €50,000 for cooperation and information-obligation breaches — a figure drawn from secondary legal commentary rather than independently re-checked against the primary legislative text. Some legal commentary describes a risk of personal liability for executives under existing German corporate-law doctrine, though this does not appear to be an explicit clause in the bill's own text.

policyAndRegulation.title: EU AI Act (as applied in Germany)
policyAndRegulation.summary: The substantive rules Germany enforces are the EU AI Act's; KI-MIG is Germany's national implementation and enforcement layer rather than a separate substantive AI statute. In 2026 the EU adopted a 'Digital Omnibus on AI' (European Parliament, 16 June 2026; Council, 29 June 2026) that postpones most high-risk AI Act obligations under Annex III from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and product-embedded (Annex I) high-risk obligations from August 2027 to August 2028 — delaying the point at which KI-MIG's enforcement powers will have substantive high-risk obligations to apply against.

policyAndRegulation.title: National AI Strategy (Strategie Künstliche Intelligenz der Bundesregierung)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Adopted 15 November 2018 and updated in December 2020 (raising planned federal AI investment to €5B by 2025), Germany's National AI Strategy was followed by a November 2023 AI Action Plan committing over €1.6B in additional funding through 2024, focused on healthcare, climate, robotics and education. The strategy and the 2023 Action Plan were issued under the ministry's predecessor (then BMBF, since restructured into BMFTR) under a previous minister; BMFTR is now led by Minister Dorothee Bär, in office since May 2025.

researchEcosystem.summary: German AI research is anchored by institutions such as DFKI (German Research Center for AI, founded 1988, led by CEO Prof. Dr. Antonio Krüger since 2019, with sites across Kaiserslautern, Saarbrücken, Bremen, Oldenburg, Osnabrück, Berlin, Darmstadt, Lübeck and Trier) and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems (which uses a distributed leadership structure across several directors rather than a single institute head), alongside university-linked hubs such as the Tübingen AI Center, Cyber Valley and the closely related but distinct ELLIS Institute Tübingen (founded 2023). Reported staff figures for DFKI vary by source and by whether graduate students are included, ranging from roughly 900 researchers to over 1,500 total employees. Some secondary sources describe German AI startups as attracting substantial funding (on the order of €1.7B in Q1 2026 per one Crunchbase-sourced figure, though it remains unclear whether that figure is AI-specific or spans all sectors), and some rank Germany highly by AI startup count, though a specific 'fourth globally' ranking could not be independently verified.

companies.name: Aleph Alpha
companies.description: German AI company focused on sovereign, enterprise-grade language models; announced a merger with Canada's Cohere in April 2026 to form a combined ~$20B transatlantic entity, not yet closed as of mid-2026.

companies.name: DeepL
companies.description: Cologne-based AI company known for high-quality machine translation; most recently valued at roughly $2B (2024) and made a further acquisition (Mixhalo) in June 2026.

companies.name: Helsing
companies.description: Munich-based defense-AI company building the HX-2 strike drone and Altra battlefield-AI software; raised a $1.8B Series E in July 2026 at an $18B valuation.

companies.name: Black Forest Labs
companies.description: Freiburg im Breisgau-based generative-AI company founded in 2024 by former Stability AI researchers, maker of the FLUX text-to-image model family; raised a $300M Series B at a $3.25B valuation in late 2025.

companies.name: SAP
companies.description: German enterprise-software company; announced the acquisition of German AI startup Prior Labs in May 2026, committing over €1B over four years to build it into a frontier tabular-AI lab for Europe (reported completed around mid-July 2026), and separately partnered with OpenAI and Microsoft on 'OpenAI for Germany' (first announced September 2025), a sovereign public-sector AI offering running on SAP's Delos Cloud.

companies.name: Celonis
companies.description: Munich-based process-mining and AI-driven business-operations software company, reportedly Germany's most valuable startup, with a private valuation reported in the roughly $11-13B range and a US IPO still anticipated (though not yet completed) as of mid-2026. Frequently cited alongside Aleph Alpha, Helsing, Black Forest Labs and DeepL in 'top German AI company' roundups, though it is sometimes categorized primarily as enterprise software/analytics rather than core AI.

companies.name: Neura Robotics
companies.description: Riederich (near Stuttgart)-based humanoid/AI-robotics company, maker of the 4NE1 humanoid robot (developed with Studio F.A. Porsche); raised a Series C reportedly of up to $1.4B in June 2026 — reportedly the largest single financing round raised by a company in Germany — at a valuation of roughly $7B, with backers including Tether, Amazon, Nvidia and Qualcomm, alongside partnerships with Bosch, AWS and TU Munich.

providers.name: Microsoft Azure
providers.description: One of the leading cloud providers for German enterprise and public-sector AI workloads.

providers.name: AWS
providers.description: Major cloud provider with significant German data-centre presence.

providers.name: Google Cloud
providers.description: Cloud provider used across German research and enterprise AI deployments.

providers.name: Hetzner
providers.description: German-owned hosting and cloud provider (Falkenstein, Nuremberg, Helsinki data centres) offering GPU cloud and dedicated servers for AI workloads.

providers.name: Deutsche Telekom / T-Systems
providers.description: Operates an 'Industrial AI Cloud' with NVIDIA at a Munich data centre, reportedly targeting over 1,000 DGX B200 systems and up to 10,000 Blackwell GPUs, alongside a sovereign 'T Cloud Public' platform.

providers.name: IONOS
providers.description: German-headquartered cloud provider marketed on EU/German data sovereignty.

providers.name: SAP Delos Cloud
providers.description: SAP's sovereign-cloud subsidiary, running atop Azure infrastructure, underpinning the 'OpenAI for Germany' public-sector AI offering.

providers.name: STACKIT
providers.description: Schwarz Group-owned cloud provider positioning itself as a 'sovereign' European cloud and AI infrastructure option; operates multiple data centres in Germany and Austria and has announced plans to expand AI/GPU capacity, though its self-described ambition to become 'Europe's first hyperscaler' has not been independently verified.

providers.name: Oracle Cloud
providers.description: US hyperscaler with a growing German presence, including a Frankfurt commercial region and an EU Sovereign Cloud region, and reported plans for a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar investment in German and Dutch AI/cloud infrastructure.

providers.name: OVHcloud
providers.description: French cloud provider with a German availability zone in Berlin and a stated strategic push into sovereign/frontier AI infrastructure as a European alternative to US hyperscalers.

providers.name: Alibaba Cloud
providers.description: Chinese hyperscaler with a minor, lower-profile data-centre presence in Germany (a Frankfurt facility, its third German site as of a 2022 expansion); a much smaller player in Germany than the major US and German providers listed above.

computeFrontier.compute: Strong public HPC (JUPITER exascale at Jülich); Deutsche Telekom/NVIDIA 'Industrial AI Cloud' in Munich
computeFrontier.chipAccess: Import-reliant; no leading-edge domestic AI-chip fab (Intel Magdeburg cancelled; ESMC Dresden targets mainstream nodes)

universities.name: DFKI
universities.description: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, founded 1988, with sites across multiple German cities. Reported staff figures vary by source (roughly 900 researchers to over 1,500 total employees including graduate students).

universities.name: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems
universities.description: Leading research institute for machine learning and robotics, based in Stuttgart and Tübingen; led by a distributed group of directors (Michael J. Black, Moritz Hardt, Bernhard Schölkopf, Katherine J. Kuchenbecker) rather than a single institute head.

universities.name: Tübingen AI Center / Cyber Valley
universities.description: Research consortium closely tied to the University of Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, described as one of Europe's largest AI research hubs by number of ML research groups and PhD students/postdocs.

universities.name: ELLIS Institute Tübingen
universities.description: European AI research institute founded in 2023, closely linked to the Tübingen AI Center and Cyber Valley ecosystem.

thinkTanks.name: interface
thinkTanks.description: Berlin-based technology policy think tank covering digital and AI governance issues; rebranded from Stiftung Neue Verantwortung in 2024.

thinkTanks.name: AlgorithmWatch
thinkTanks.description: Berlin/Zurich-based NGO focused on algorithmic accountability, AI ethics and AI-policy advocacy across Europe.

thinkTanks.name: Alexander von Humboldt Institute for Internet and Society (HIIG)
thinkTanks.description: Berlin-based research institute (founded 2011, backed by Humboldt Universität zu Berlin, Berlin University of the Arts and WZB) working at the intersection of internet/AI research and policy, including projects such as 'Shaping AI' and the Internet Policy Review journal.

governmentInstitutions.name: Federal Ministry for Digital Transformation and Government Modernisation (BMDS)
governmentInstitutions.description: Germany's first dedicated federal digital ministry, established by the Chancellor's organisational decree of 6 May 2025; led by Dr. Karsten Wildberger since its creation.

governmentInstitutions.name: Bundesnetzagentur
governmentInstitutions.description: Named as Germany's lead market-surveillance authority for AI Act enforcement under the new KI-MIG law, with BaFin covering financial-sector AI and BfDI retaining data-protection oversight. President Klaus Müller has led the agency since March 2022.

governmentInstitutions.name: BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority)
governmentInstitutions.description: Covers AI oversight within Germany's financial sector, working alongside the Bundesnetzagentur under the KI-MIG enforcement framework.

governmentInstitutions.name: BfDI (Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information)
governmentInstitutions.description: Retains data-protection oversight of AI systems under the KI-MIG enforcement framework. Prof. Dr. Moritz Hennemann was elected by the Bundestag as the next Federal Commissioner on 25 June 2026, but as of the most recent research had not yet taken office; incumbent Louisa Specht-Riemenschneider, who is stepping down for health reasons, remains the acting Federal Commissioner through 30 September 2026.

governmentInstitutions.name: Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR)
governmentInstitutions.description: Ministry responsible for Germany's National AI Strategy and AI Action Plan; led by Minister Dorothee Bär since May 2025.

debates.topic: Executive liability risk under Germany's AI Act enforcement framework
debates.summary: Some commentary describes KI-MIG as creating personal liability for executives over AI security failures, but direct summaries of the bill's own text describe only new enforcement authorities and modest national fines — the liability narrative appears to trace to separate legal analysis of existing German corporate-law doctrine rather than a specific clause in KI-MIG itself.
debates.expanded: KI-MIG's own text names Bundesnetzagentur, BaFin and BfDI as enforcement authorities and adds supplementary national fines of up to €50,000 for cooperation and information-obligation breaches; legal-analysis sources reviewed do not describe an explicit personal-liability clause in the bill. Separate commentary (e.g. from February 2026) argues that established doctrines such as Organisationsverschulden and Geschäftsführerhaftung could expose executives' private assets if they fail to implement adequate AI Act compliance oversight — a risk analysis derived from general corporate law meeting new EU AI Act duties, rather than a liability clause introduced by KI-MIG. Some industry voices have nonetheless expressed concern that this combination could push AI deployment decisions toward excessive caution or offshore structuring, while others argue it is a reasonable reading of existing law rather than a new legal risk.

debates.topic: Germany's sovereign AI champion merges with a foreign partner
debates.summary: Aleph Alpha's planned merger with Canada's Cohere has prompted debate about what 'sovereign AI' means when a national champion combines with a foreign lab, even though the deal had not closed as of mid-2026.
debates.expanded: Aleph Alpha had been positioned for years as Germany's answer to dependence on US and French AI labs. Founder Jonas Andrulis stepped down as CEO on 10 October 2025 and became chairman of the company's advisory board. Reto Spörri had already joined as co-CEO alongside Andrulis in July 2025, and Ilhan Scheer was appointed a second co-CEO effective 1 February 2026, shortly before the Cohere transaction was announced (some later coverage describes both co-CEO appointments as dating to February 2026, which appears to understate Spörri's actual tenure). The April 2026 merger agreement — announced alongside a new Germany-Canada tech alliance — would create a combined ~$20B transatlantic entity anchored in Berlin and Toronto; if it closes, some observers argue German enterprise and public-sector AI deployments (like the Federal Employment Agency's helpdesk, built on Aleph Alpha's Pharia OS) would increasingly run on jointly or foreign-owned technology, even if from a close ally.

debates.summary: A new alliance with Canada aims to deepen cooperation on sovereign technology capability between the two countries — launched in the same period as Canada's Cohere agreed to merge with Aleph Alpha, an AI lab often described as one of Germany's leading sovereign AI ventures.
debates.expanded: Launched via a Joint Declaration of Intent on AI signed by Digital Minister Karsten Wildberger and Canada's AI/Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon on the margins of the February 2026 Munich Security Conference, building on a December 2025 Canada-Germany Digital Alliance, the alliance's practical meaning is still being worked out — particularly given the Cohere-Aleph Alpha merger running in parallel.

debates.topic: AI training data and copyright (GEMA v. Suno)
debates.summary: The Regional Court of Munich I's reported 31 July 2026 ruling that AI music generator Suno infringed GEMA-held copyright — in both training and output — is described as Europe's first such decision and sharpens the German and EU debate over whether text-and-data-mining exceptions cover generative-AI training.
debates.expanded: The court reportedly found six well-known works 'memorised' within Suno's v3.5 and v4 models and recognisable in their outputs, rejected reliance on a TDM exception for the training, and held Suno — as the operator that chose the training data and architecture — liable for infringing outputs rather than the users who wrote the prompts. It ordered disclosure of revenues and left damages to a later proceeding. Coming days before the EU AI Act's 2 August GPAI-transparency milestone (which requires marking of AI-generated content but does not itself resolve training-data licensing), the ruling is provisionally enforceable but not final, and Suno may appeal to the Munich Higher Regional Court. Rights-holders frame it as vindicating a licensing-first model for AI training, while some developers warn it could push model training offshore; it sits alongside GEMA's parallel actions against other generative-AI providers.

notableGaps.note: Germany's National Security Council announced on 9 June 2026 that it intends to establish an AI safety institute modeled on the UK's AISI, beginning as a 'virtual institution' before a permanent site is chosen. As of the most recent research, no formal institute name, budget or legal basis had been confirmed — some industry/press commentary has informally used the label 'DE-AISI', but this is not an official designation — so in the interim oversight remains distributed across the Bundesnetzagentur (market surveillance), BaFin (financial-sector AI) and BfDI (data protection).

notableGaps.area: Domestic AI compute and chip fabrication
notableGaps.note: Intel's planned ~€30B Magdeburg 'mega-fab' was cancelled in 2025. The TSMC-led ESMC joint venture (with Bosch, Infineon and NXP) building a fab in Dresden and Infineon's new Dresden 'Smart Power Fab' target mainstream/power-management nodes rather than leading-edge AI compute chips, leaving Germany without domestic leading-edge chip fabrication for frontier AI hardware. Germany does host significant AI-relevant supercomputing capacity, however, including the JUPITER EuroHPC exascale system at Forschungszentrum Jülich (operational since mid-2025 and ranked among the world's most powerful systems), which is used for both scientific and AI workloads.

No lab headquartered in Germany currently trains an independent, general-purpose frontier-scale foundation model comparable to GPT/Gemini/Claude-class systems. Aleph Alpha was the closest domestic contender, but its planned merger with Canada's Cohere — if it closes — would fold its model development into a combined transatlantic entity rather than a purely German one, and no new independent frontier-model contender was identified in recent research.
